summary: Anemone coronaria, the poppy anemone, is a tuber-forming herbaceous perennial native to the Mediterranean region. Its solitary flowers typically have five to eight showy red, white or blue petal-like tepals around a dark centre, whose crown-like ring of stamens inspired the species name. In its native range it blooms from winter to early spring and is cross-pollinated by bees, flies and beetles, with different flower colours attracting different visitors.

Rhinanthus minor, or yellow rattle, is an annual wildflower distributed across Europe, western Asia and northern North America. It is a hemiparasite: its roots tap neighbouring plants, especially grasses and legumes, for nutrients. By suppressing dominant grasses it can help other meadow flowers establish, so it is used in grassland restoration, although farmers may regard the same effect as a loss of hay yield. Its loose seeds rattle inside ripe capsules.
reviewFlags: Animal toxicity is described only as a reputation in the source.

summary: Geranium molle, the dove's-foot crane's-bill, is a small, hairy annual in the geranium family. Its branched stems carry rounded, deeply divided leaves and small pinkish-purple flowers with jagged petals, blooming from April to September. It grows in dry meadows, hedges, banks and woodland edges, favouring sunny places with sandy, relatively dry soil. The flowers contain both male and female structures and are mainly pollinated by bees, wasps and their relatives.

Campsis radicans, the American trumpet vine, is a vigorous deciduous woody vine native to eastern North America. Aerial rootlets and twining stems let it climb trees and structures, while its orange to reddish-orange trumpet-shaped flowers attract hummingbirds and other nectar feeders. Once largely associated with swampy bottomlands, it has also colonised thickets, fence lines and abandoned farmland, and its dense growth can cover other plants or buildings.

Prunus laurocerasus, the cherry laurel, is an evergreen cherry native to lands around the Black Sea in southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia. It has glossy, leathery leaves that may smell of almonds when crushed, sweet-smelling clusters of creamy-white flowers, and small fruits that turn black when ripe. Its laurel name comes from its resemblance to bay laurel, although the two plants are not closely related.

summary: Tordylium apulum, the Mediterranean hartwort, is an annual herb in the carrot family, native to Europe and western Asia. It grows in cultivated ground, waste places and roadsides across sandy, loamy and clay soils, but does not thrive in shade. Its white flower heads have enlarged, deeply two-lobed outer petals, followed by round, flattened and elaborately textured fruits. The leaves are eaten as a pot herb or salad vegetable in Greece and used as a condiment in Italy.

Rhamnus lycioides, the Mediterranean buckthorn, is a tangled, thorny shrub of southern Europe and northern Africa adapted to the dry Mediterranean climate. It tolerates drought, rocky nutrient-poor ground, overgrazing and trampling, and can persist as a pioneer in degraded drylands. Individuals within one population may fruit in different months, extending the supply of berries for the birds that disperse its seeds; its branches also provide small birds with nesting shelter.

Pereskia aculeata, the Barbados gooseberry, is a scrambling cactus native to tropical America. Unlike the familiar leafless, succulent form of many cacti, it has large leaves, spiny non-succulent stems and strongly scented pale flowers. Its leaves and fruits are eaten, and the leaves are a popular vegetable in parts of Minas Gerais, Brazil. Where introduced in South Africa, it can form impenetrable clumps that smother native trees and regrow from leaves or stem pieces.

Clarkia unguiculata, the elegant clarkia, is a wildflower endemic to California, where it grows in oak woodlands and on dry open or lightly shaded slopes. Its four slender, paddle-like petals range from pink to reddish purple, framing long stamens with prominent red anthers and a projecting stigma. A native bee, Hesperapis regularis, is its main pollinator, but the plant can also self-pollinate. Its small fruit holds many seeds.

details.use: eaten or ground into a fine powder

summary: Limonium dodartii is a flowering plant in the leadwort family. In mainland Portugal it is confined to rocky greywacke sea cliffs on the southwestern Alentejo coast. A 2016–2019 assessment classified the Portuguese population as Vulnerable, citing its very small range, reproductive problems and threats from coastal erosion, trampling and invasive plants. Suggested conservation work included protecting its habitat, storing genetic material, nursery propagation and regular monitoring.

Chrysojasminum fruticans, the wild jasmine, is a semi-evergreen shrub native from the Mediterranean region east to northern Iran. Its yellow flowers occur in small terminal clusters and come in two forms: one has short styles and long stamens, the other long styles and short stamens. The plant cannot pollinate itself or produce viable seed with the same flower form, yet it also spreads clonally through rhizomes. Bees, flies, moths and butterflies visit its flowers.

Narcissus gaditanus is a bulb-forming daffodil endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. In mainland Portugal it occurs only in the Algarve, on rocky limestone ground and outcrops. A 2016–2019 assessment classified the national population as Vulnerable, estimating fewer than 10,000 mature plants and an ongoing decline. Reported threats included irrigated agriculture, limestone quarrying, development and illegal bulb collection.
reviewFlags: The population estimate and status are from a 2016–2019 mainland Portugal assessment.

summary: Iris domestica, the blackberry lily, is a rhizomatous perennial native to eastern Asia. Its orange-red flowers are scattered with darker spots and bloom in summer; in autumn, opened pods reveal clusters of shiny black seeds resembling blackberries. It grows wild in grasslands, pastures, forest clearings, meadows, mountains and shrublands. Once the sole species of the genus Belamcanda, it was transferred to Iris in 2005 following DNA evidence.

Pellia epiphylla, the common pellia, is a thallose liverwort found across North America, Europe, North Africa and parts of Asia. It forms green, irregularly branched patches in damp, sheltered places, especially beside streams and ditches or in wet woodland. Fertilisation depends on water: the male organs burst when wet, releasing swimming sperm. The resulting spore-producing plant remains attached to the larger green plant until its capsule matures and splits.

Gagea pratensis, the yellow star-of-Bethlehem, is a bulb-forming perennial native across much of Europe and the Mediterranean, including Turkey and Morocco. Its flowers are usually yellow, sometimes with a green stripe behind each tepal. In mainland Portugal it reaches the edge of its range on rocky soils in the Serra da Nogueira. A 2016–2019 assessment found only two Portuguese locations and classified the species there as Vulnerable.
reviewFlags: The location count and status are from a 2016–2019 mainland Portugal assessment.

summary: Lophostemon confertus, the brush box, is an evergreen tree native to coastal Queensland and northeastern New South Wales in Australia. Its form changes markedly with exposure: in moist open forest and at rainforest edges it can exceed 40 metres, while on coastal headlands it becomes stunted and wind-sheared. Its dense crown of dark green, leathery leaves casts deep shade, and the species is widely planted as a street tree in Australian cities.

Rumex spinosus, the devil's thorn or spiny dock, is an annual herb originating in the warmer parts of the Old World and now spread elsewhere by people. It favours disturbed, especially sandy, ground and grows as a sprawling weed. Its many seeds have hard, prickly casings; some form along the branches and others at the stem base, where the drying root pulls them into the ground at the end of the plant's life.
Genista micrantha is a flowering plant in the pea family, endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and present in mainland Portugal.

Cotoneaster horizontalis, the wall cotoneaster, is a low, spreading shrub native to mountains of Nepal, China and Taiwan. It is cultivated for flat, symmetrical sprays of small glossy leaves, with pink to white flowers appearing in summer, and is commonly used as groundcover or hedging. The species has naturalised in parts of the United Kingdom and has also been recorded in Ireland, with some concern that it may be becoming invasive.

Lemna minuta, the least duckweed, is the smallest species of Lemna and is native to an uncertain part of the Americas. Each tiny plant is a translucent green oval in shade but generally grows in pairs in full sun, and its flower is brief and membrane-bound. It floats on calm or stagnant fresh water, where dense surface mats can reduce both sunlight penetration and oxygen exchange.

Luculia gratissima is a flowering shrub or small tree found from the central Himalayas to northern Indochina. It can reach about four metres tall and bears pointed, ribbed leaves and clusters of fragrant pale pink flowers in autumn and winter. Grown as an ornamental, it cannot tolerate temperatures below about 5°C and therefore needs protected cultivation in temperate regions.

Pachystachys lutea, the golden shrimp plant, is a soft-stemmed tropical evergreen shrub native to Peru. Its short-lived white flowers emerge one after another from overlapping bright yellow bracts throughout the warm months. It is cultivated as an ornamental, but needs protection from temperatures below about 10°C in cold temperate regions.

Arctotis stoechadifolia, the white arctotis or African daisy, is a South African flowering plant found in coastal sand dunes along the western Cape. The source describes it as rare within that native range and records an introduction to New Zealand. Its taxonomic boundary is unsettled: some treatments combine it with the more widespread Arctotis venusta, while others recognise the two as distinct species.
reviewFlags: Taxonomic treatment relative to Arctotis venusta varies.

summary: Prunella laciniata, the cut-leaved selfheal, is a plant in the mint family. It sometimes hybridises with Prunella vulgaris to form P. × intermedia, and with P. grandiflora to form P. × dissecta.

Malva tournefortiana, the Pyrenees mallow, is a flowering plant in the mallow family native to Morocco, Portugal, Spain and France. It is a hexaploid member of the same section as Malva moschata and Malva alcea.
